newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China buying a "green" fuel oil over rust fears.
newsitem.headline: China buying a "green" fuel oil over rust fears.

text.p: China's import demand for a "green" fuel oil is rising because of power station fears over rust, industry sources said on Wednesday.
They said China had moved away from importing 3.5 percent sulphur fuel oil to buying more 1.5-2.0 percent grade fuel oil in the benchmark Singapore spot market.
Sulphur is the most corrosive element for refineries to deal with, as well as being a major contributor to pollution.
China has long imported only occasional cargoes of lower sulphur fuel oil from Russia, but now it is importing the product from Singapore, South Korea and Japan.
Singapore traders said they estimated China had bought up to 300,000 tonnes of the lower sulphur fuel oil in the last few weeks. The fuel oil will arrive in June and July.

They said most of it was for Shanghai, China's biggest city, and power companies in Guangdong in the south. China's refineries already produce the lower sulphur grade, but the rising domestic demand has led to the need for imports.
Traders in Beijing and Singapore said the move was motivated by concerns among power plants of corrosion caused by using higher sulphur grade fuel oil as a feedstock.
Chinese importers in Shanghai and Beijing said there was no new legislation guiding the move.

Li Pei, a senior official at the Chinese National Environmental Protection Agency in Beijing, told Reuters by telephone the agency was organising a committee to look into lowering the sulphur content of diesel and fuel oil used in China.
"But it would only look into the issue seriously after the year 2000 as we are currently focusing our efforts on our recent move to ban the use of leaded gasoline," she said.
Power plants in China use coal and fuel oil as feedstock. New plants which are about four to five years old, mainly in the southwest, run on imported fuel oil due to a shortage of domestic supplies.
Analysts in Shanghai said there was a move among China's refiners to install facilities to make lower-sulphur oil products to try to meet the rising demand for cleaner fuels.
The recent spurt of enquiries for lower sulphur grade fuel oil taken some traders by surprise.

"They have usually been importing the high sulphur supplies from Singapore, South Korea and Japan, though they sometimes take in the medium sulphur grades from Russia as they are cheap," said one Japanese trader in Singapore.
Traders who were holding on to their high sulphur fuel oil stocks in anticipation of higher prices were caught out by the recent Chinese import demand.
"We have to blend the high sulphur grades to lower sulphur supplies. But that represents a cost and few Chinese buyers are willing to pay the higher price," said a Singapore-based trader.
The trader said blending costs were at least US $2-$3 per tonne.
China imports an average of between 400,000 tonnes to 600,000 tonnes of high sulphur fuel oil per month.
